vignette:
She is seventy-eight now, a widow who still wakes before dawn on workdays to put on her headset and log in as a call center agent from the small apartment where she has lived alone for the past twelve years. Her voice on the phone is steady and courteous, the kind of voice that knows how to calm strangers. People who speak with her hear patience, professionalism, even warmth. They do not hear the effort it takes for her to keep her breathing even when a caller raises his voice, or how quickly her heart begins to pound when a sudden beep sounds in her headset.

She traces the beginning of it back more than three decades, to a busy afternoon in the central plaza of her home city in Latin America. At that time she is in her forties, married, raising children, and working at a neighborhood stationery shop. She remembers carrying a bag of groceries and thinking about dinner when the explosion tears through the street ahead of her. At first she does not understand what has happened. Then the air changes—heat, dust, shattered glass, the metallic smell of blood, screaming from every direction. She drops to the ground without deciding to. For a few seconds she cannot hear anything but a shrill ringing. When her hearing returns, it comes back all at once: people crying for help, car alarms, someone shouting the names of the missing.

She sees bodies on the pavement. A shoe without its owner. A bus window blown outward. She remembers a child standing alone and covered in gray dust, his mouth open in a silent cry before sound catches up. She runs, then turns back, then runs again, disoriented and ashamed of being afraid. In the days that follow, she learns that the bombing was an act of terrorism, one of several that year. She was not physically injured, but for weeks she feels as if her skin has been peeled away. Every slammed door makes her jump. She starts taking side streets to avoid crowded places. At night, when her husband falls asleep beside her, she lies awake listening for engines, sirens, footsteps.

Life moves forward in the way it demands. She returns to work. She cooks, washes clothes, gets her children to school, goes to church. Outwardly she becomes known as strong. Inwardly she begins arranging her world around danger. She avoids buses and public squares. She scans every room for exits. If she notices an abandoned bag, she leaves immediately, making excuses that sound reasonable even to herself. When anniversaries of attacks are mentioned on the radio, her stomach turns and she switches the station. Sometimes an image comes back so vividly that she loses the thread of whatever she is doing. While slicing onions or folding laundry, she is suddenly back in the plaza, smelling smoke, tasting grit between her teeth.

After her husband dies, the nights grow harder. There is no one beside her to anchor her when she wakes from dreams in which the blast repeats itself or changes shape—sometimes it is the plaza, sometimes it is her apartment building, sometimes her children are still children and she cannot find them in the crowd. She gets out of bed to check the locks, then checks them again because she cannot trust the first check. Sleep becomes fragmented. In the morning she feels old in a way that is more than age.

She takes the call center job after widowhood because she needs the income and because she likes the structure. She tells herself that speaking to customers from home will be easier than facing the unpredictability of the outside world. In some ways it is. She can keep the curtains at the angle she prefers and sit with her back to the wall. But the work also exposes how little control she feels she truly has. A dropped call tone can mimic an alarm in just the wrong way. An irate customer’s sudden shouting sends a jolt through her body so strong that she has to mute herself and press her hand against her chest. She keeps a glass of water nearby because her mouth goes dry when she is startled. Her supervisors know her as conscientious, but they do not know that after particularly difficult calls she sits in silence, waiting for the trembling in her hands to stop.

Her children, now grown, tell her she worries too much. She does not disagree. She worries when they travel, when there are news reports of violence, when she hears motorcycles revving beneath her window. She avoids holiday festivals and crowded markets she once loved. Even church is difficult on feast days when too many people pack into the pews. She sits near the back, close to the door, and scans faces without meaning to. She hates that she does this. She says she is tired of living as if something terrible is always about to happen, yet that feeling remains constant, low and electrical, inside her body.

What troubles her most is that the event is both far away and permanently present. She knows, rationally, that she survived and that she is an old woman in a quiet apartment speaking to customers about bills and service plans. Yet a siren in the street or a breaking-news alert on television can collapse the years in an instant. Then she is again that woman in the plaza, crouched amid smoke and confusion, trying to understand how an ordinary afternoon becomes a scene of horror before a person has time to protect herself.
